techniques.name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
techniques.description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

example_use_cases.description: An estate agency's data team standardises the inputs of a linear house-price model, then ranks the absolute coefficients to show valuers which property attributes move the estimate most. Valuers check that the signs match their experience, for example that more floor area raises the price, before the model guides asking prices.

A lender's model-risk team documents a linear credit-scoring model for its regulator by publishing the standardised coefficient of every input. The reviewer can read off the direction and relative weight of each input without a separate explanation tool, and can query any input that carries more weight than policy allows.

A public health analyst fits a logistic regression to predict emergency readmission and reports standardised coefficients to clinicians, who see which patient characteristics push the predicted risk up or down. The analyst refits on resamples first, to check that the large coefficients keep their sign.

limitations.description: Raw magnitudes have output-per-input units and cannot be ranked across differently scaled variables. Express comparable input changes explicitly; changing metres to centimetres makes the corresponding coefficient smaller for the same predictions.

Coefficients concern the encoded model inputs while other inputs are held fixed. If the model includes transformed variables or interactions, inspecting one coefficient does not give the whole effect of changing an original variable.

Correlated predictors can have unstable or shared coefficients even when predictions change little. Scaling does not remove this problem, and regularisation can change which correlated feature receives a large weight.

Each coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model. A feature can have a negative coefficient while rising with the outcome on its own, so a coefficient read in isolation can mislead about the feature's plain relationship to the outcome.

A coefficient is a conditional association in the fitted model, not a causal effect. Its magnitude alone also does not give a particular applicant's contribution, which depends on that applicant's feature values.

techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

example_use_cases.description: A model-risk team at a bank fits a ridge surrogate to a gradient-boosted credit-scoring model's scores on a held-out sample, reports how closely the surrogate reproduces them, and uses the standardised coefficients to brief the model-risk committee on which inputs drive scores overall.

A hospital analytics team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural network that predicts readmission risk from tabular records, to check that the features driving the network's predictions overall, such as age and prior admissions, are plausible to clinicians. The findings concern the network, not what causes readmission.

An energy company's forecasting team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural-network load forecaster using a year of hourly weather and calendar inputs, and reads the standardised coefficients to confirm that temperature and time of day dominate. A low R-squared during heatwaves leads the team to record that the surrogate does not describe the model in that regime.

An insurer's compliance team gives a regulator a ridge surrogate of its pricing model together with held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, so the regulator can check the stated drivers against the model's actual outputs.

limitations.description: A linear surrogate cannot represent interactions or thresholds. Where the complex model relies on them, the surrogate fits its predictions poorly and its coefficients describe a different model. Report held-out R-squared and treat a low value as a failed surrogate.

A good average fit can hide poor fit in parts of the input space, such as rare groups or extreme values, so the coefficients may be wrong for exactly the cases that matter. Check fidelity within subgroups and near decision boundaries.
There is no agreed fidelity level above which a surrogate can be trusted. Whether 50%, 80% or 99% of variance explained is enough depends on the use, so the reviewer has to set and justify a cut-off.

Ridge shrinks every coefficient and shares weight between correlated features. Coefficient sizes depend on the penalty strength and on feature scaling, so compare them only after standardising the features, and report the penalty used.

The surrogate explains the complex model's behaviour on the sampled inputs, not the real-world link between features and outcomes. Reading its coefficients as causes, or as evidence about the data, will mislead.

techniques.name: Partial Dependence Plots
techniques.description: Partial Dependence Plots show how changing one or two features affects a model's predictions on average. The technique works by varying the selected feature(s) across their full range whilst keeping all other features fixed at their original values, then averaging the predictions. This creates a clear visualisation of whether increasing or decreasing a feature tends to increase or decrease predictions, and reveals patterns like linear trends, plateaus, or threshold effects that help explain model behaviour.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing how house prices change with property size in a real estate prediction model, revealing whether the relationship is linear or if there are diminishing returns for very large properties.
Examining how customer age affects predicted loan default probability in a credit scoring model, showing whether risk increases steadily with age or has specific age ranges with higher risk.
Visualising how temperature affects crop yield predictions in agricultural models, identifying optimal temperature ranges and potential threshold effects.

limitations.description: Assumes the plotted features are independent of the others. When they are correlated, the averaging pairs values that never occur together, so the curve partly reflects how the model behaves in regions with no data.

Shows only the average effect. If a feature acts in opposite directions for different groups of instances, the effects cancel and the curve can look flat, so interactions with other features stay hidden.
Limited to one or two features at a time, because higher-dimensional plots cannot be read. Effects that depend on three or more features together cannot be shown.
The basic method needs a pass over the whole dataset for every grid value, so cost grows with dataset size, the number of grid points and the time the model takes to predict.

resources.title: Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine.
resources.abstract: Function estimation/approximation is viewed from the perspective of numerical optimization in function space, rather than parameter space. A connection is made between stagewise additive expansions and steepest-descent minimization. A general gradient descent “boosting” paradigm is developed for additive expansions based on any fitting criterion.Specific algorithms are presented for least-squares, least absolute deviation, and Huber-M loss functions for regression, and multiclass logistic likelihood for classification. Special enhancements are derived for the particular case where the individual additive components are regression trees, and tools for interpreting such “TreeBoost” models are presented. Gradient boosting of regression trees produces competitive, highly robust, interpretable procedures for both regression and classification, especially appropriate for mining less than clean data. Connections between this approach and the boosting methods of Freund and Shapire and Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani are discussed.

resources.title: Using machine learning to examine freight network spatial vulnerabilities to disasters: A new take on partial dependence plots
resources.abstract: Analyzing transportation network vulnerabilities to disruptions is crucial for society to maintain commodity flows across the globe. However, most vulnerability analyses focus on impacts that arise from the deterioration of single network components, which can overlook spatial correlations between multiple components that manifest during area-spanning disruptions, such as those stemming from natural hazards. Here, we demonstrate an intuitive, simulation-based approach for inferring spatial vulnerabilities to area-spanning disruptions. In particular, we show how partial dependence plots derived from gradient boosting machines trained on the results of a routing simulation can be used to depict the average effect a disruption’s location has on impacts while controlling for other input variables and spatial dependencies embedded in the network. Although we demonstrate our approach for Middle Tennessee’s intermodal road and rail freight transportation network, our framework can easily be applied to other networks.

resources.title: Uncovering nonlinear patterns in time-sensitive prehospital breathing emergencies: an exploratory machine learning study
resources.abstract: Background Timely prehospital care is crucial for patients presenting with high-risk time-sensitive (HRTS) conditions. However, the interplay between response time and demographic factors in patients with breathing problems remains insufficiently understood. In this exploratory study, we applied machine learning (ML) to examine how emergency medical response time, age, and sex jointly influence the probability of encountering HRTS conditions. Methods A retrospective observational analysis was conducted on 132,395 prehospital missions in Stockholm (2017–2022). Multiple ML models, random forest, gradient boosting, neural networks, and logistic regression were trained to probe potential nonlinear patterns and interactions, not with the primary goal of predictive accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC) measures. However, partial dependence (PD) and individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots were the principal tools illustrating how response time, age, and sex shape HRTS likelihood. Results PD and ICE plots revealed that older age (> 60 years) was consistently associated with a higher probability of HRTS. Moreover, patients over 60 years displayed a complex, rising risk at prolonged response times exceeding two hours. Gradient boosting offered the best (though modest) classification metrics, with an AUC of 0.66 and an F1-score of 0.55. We emphasize that these metrics, while necessary for completeness, were secondary to our aim of characterizing nonlinear relationships. Conclusions Our findings underscore the exploratory value of ML in identifying subtle relationships and interactions among response time, age, and sex for time-sensitive breathing emergencies. These results highlight opportunities to refine dispatch protocols, develop age- and sex-focused screening questions, and revisit lower-priority calls after extended wait times. Future work should incorporate richer data and refine these insights for potential predictive use. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

techniques.name: Gradient Saliency
techniques.description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers: it takes the gradient of the score for a chosen class (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass, to show which pixels that score is most sensitive to. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are drawn for the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see whether the sensitive pixels sit on a cue linked to that group; the group-wise errors come from a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital imaging team validating a pneumonia detection model on chest X-rays computes gradient saliency for a sample of confirmed cases and checks whether the most sensitive pixels lie over the lungs rather than over tubes, monitoring leads or position markers. They use the result to decide whether the model is ready for a clinical pilot or needs retraining on cleaner images.

An agricultural technology company testing a plant disease classifier on leaf photographs taken in the field computes gradient saliency for the images it misclassifies. It checks whether the sensitive pixels sit on the diseased leaf area or on soil, trays and hands in the frame, and decides whether to collect photographs with more varied backgrounds.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It then inspects gradient saliency on those errors. Where the most sensitive pixels sit on faces and hair rather than on uniforms or equipment, the model is using appearance linked to gender as a shortcut, so the team rebalances the training photographs and retrains.

limitations.description: Maps are noisy and can change sharply for tiny changes to the image, so one map is weak evidence. A study of upper-limb X-ray classifiers found that plain-gradient maps were less accurate at locating abnormalities, and less repeatable, than radiologists' markings (Venkatesh et al., 2024). Look at many images and more than one trained model before drawing a conclusion about the model.

The gradient is local. Where the model's output has flattened, for example once a feature is already strongly present, the gradient is near zero, so a pixel the model relies on can get almost no score. Sundararajan et al. (2017) show this with a one-ReLU example, which is why methods such as Integrated Gradients measure the change from a baseline instead.

Because only the size of each gradient is kept, the map cannot say whether a pixel supports or counts against the chosen class. Evidence that argues against the prediction looks the same as evidence for it, so a map cannot show that a pixel was used in the way a reviewer assumes.

A high score means the output is sensitive to a small change in that pixel, not that the model relied on it or that removing it would change the decision. Pixel-level scores are scattered and often capture only the most discriminative part of an object (Simonyan et al., 2013), so they rarely outline a whole lesion or object a reviewer can name.

resources.title: Deep Inside Convolutional Networks: Visualising Image Classification Models and Saliency Maps
resources.abstract: This paper addresses the visualisation of image classification models, learnt using deep Convolutional Networks (ConvNets). We consider two visualisation techniques, based on computing the gradient of the class score with respect to the input image. The first one generates an image, which maximises the class score [Erhan et al., 2009], thus visualising the notion of the class, captured by a ConvNet. The second technique computes a class saliency map, specific to a given image and class. We show that such maps can be employed for weakly supervised object segmentation using classification ConvNets. Finally, we establish the connection between the gradient-based ConvNet visualisation methods and deconvolutional networks [Zeiler et al., 2013].

resources.title: Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

techniques.name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
techniques.description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

example_use_cases.description: A dermatology AI team validating a melanoma classifier overlays Grad-CAM on dermoscopy images and compares the highlighted region with the lesion outline drawn by a clinician. Cases where the heat falls on a ruler, hair or skin markings are collected, and the team decides whether the training images need cleaning before the model goes to clinical evaluation.

A team developing the traffic sign recogniser for a driver assistance system overlays Grad-CAM on the test images it misclassifies. When the heat sits on the background or a shadow rather than on the sign, they add training images with similar backgrounds and lighting, then recheck the overlays before the release decision.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It overlays Grad-CAM on those errors: heat on faces and hairstyles rather than on uniforms or equipment shows the model has learned a gender shortcut, and a count of the training photographs by gender shows why. The team rebalances the photographs, retrains and checks that the heat moves.

limitations.description: Needs the network's gradients and its last convolutional feature maps, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an API, or on architectures without convolutional layers. The user must also choose which layer to use, and the paper reports that maps become progressively worse for earlier layers (Selvaraju et al., Sec 3).

The map has the resolution of the last convolutional layer (14 by 14 for VGG-16 and AlexNet), then is enlarged to the image. Small or irregular findings, such as a few-millimetre lesion or a thin sign pole, fall inside one or two cells, so the overlay cannot show whether the model attended to the finding or to its surroundings.

In a chest X-ray benchmark Grad-CAM generally located pathologies better than six other saliency methods but worse than radiologists, with the largest gap for small, complex-shaped findings, and it located them better when the model was confident (Saporta et al., 2022). The overlays are least reliable for the uncertain, hard cases where a reviewer most wants an explanation.

A bright region means features there raise the class score under a local linear approximation, not that the model relied on them. In the paper's own check, Grad-CAM's ranking of image patches agreed only moderately with occlusion, which masks patches and re-scores the image (rank correlation 0.254, Sec 5.3). The ReLU also hides regions that count against the class.

resources.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization
resources.abstract: We propose a technique for producing "visual explanations" for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models, making them more transparent. Our approach - Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), uses the gradients of any target concept, flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce a coarse localization map highlighting important regions in the image for predicting the concept. Grad-CAM is applicable to a wide variety of CNN model-families: (1) CNNs with fully-connected layers, (2) CNNs used for structured outputs, (3) CNNs used in tasks with multimodal inputs or reinforcement learning, without any architectural changes or re-training. We combine Grad-CAM with fine-grained visualizations to create a high-resolution class-discriminative visualization and apply it to off-the-shelf image classification, captioning, and visual question answering (VQA) models, including ResNet-based architectures. In the context of image classification models, our visualizations (a) lend insights into their failure modes, (b) are robust to adversarial images, (c) outperform previous methods on localization, (d) are more faithful to the underlying model and (e) help achieve generalization by identifying dataset bias. For captioning and VQA, we show that even non-attention based models can localize inputs. We devise a way to identify important neurons through Grad-CAM and combine it with neuron names to provide textual explanations for model decisions. Finally, we design and conduct human studies to measure if Grad-CAM helps users establish appropriate trust in predictions from models and show that Grad-CAM helps untrained users successfully discern a 'stronger' nodel from a 'weaker' one even when both make identical predictions. Our code is available at https://github.com/ramprs/grad-cam/, along with a demo at http://gradcam.cloudcv.org, and a video at youtu.be/COjUB9Izk6E.

resources.title: A Tutorial on Explainable Image Classification for Dementia Stages Using Convolutional Neural Network and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
resources.abstract: This paper presents a tutorial of an explainable approach using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to classify four progressive dementia stages based on open MRI brain images. The detailed implementation steps are demonstrated with an explanation. Whilst the proposed CNN architecture is demonstrated to achieve more than 99% accuracy for the test dataset, the computational procedure of CNN remains a black box. The visualisation based on Grad-CAM is attempted to explain such very high accuracy and may provide useful information for physicians. Future motivation based on this work is discussed.

resources.title: Benchmarking saliency methods for chest X-ray interpretation
resources.abstract: Saliency methods, which produce heat maps that highlight the areas of the medical image that influence model prediction, are often presented to clinicians as an aid in diagnostic decision-making. However, rigorous investigation of the accuracy and reliability of these strategies is necessary before they are integrated into the clinical setting. In this work, we quantitatively evaluate seven saliency methods, including Grad-CAM, across multiple neural network architectures using two evaluation metrics. We establish the first human benchmark for chest X-ray segmentation in a multilabel classification set-up, and examine under what clinical conditions saliency maps might be more prone to failure in localizing important pathologies compared with a human expert benchmark. We find that (1) while Grad-CAM generally localized pathologies better than the other evaluated saliency methods, all seven performed significantly worse compared with the human benchmark, (2) the gap in localization performance between Grad-CAM and the human benchmark was largest for pathologies that were smaller in size and had shapes that were more complex, and (3) model confidence was positively correlated with Grad-CAM localization performance. Our work demonstrates that several important limitations of saliency methods must be addressed before we can rely on them for deep learning explainability in medical imaging.

techniques.name: Factor Analysis
techniques.description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team finds that forty macroeconomic and credit-bureau inputs to a default-risk model are heavily correlated. Exploratory factor analysis groups them into four factors the team can name, such as growth, inflation, household debt and credit conditions, and the model is rebuilt on the factor scores so its drivers can be explained to the risk committee in four terms instead of forty.

A flood-forecasting team with sixty correlated gauge, soil-moisture and satellite inputs runs factor analysis on the training data to find a few underlying drivers, such as rainfall intensity, catchment wetness and river level. Forecast explanations are then reported per driver, which operators can relate to what they see on the ground.

limitations.description: The standard model is linear, with each variable a weighted sum of factors plus noise. Maximum-likelihood extraction also assumes roughly normal data, so skewed, binary or strongly non-linear variables can distort the loadings. Check distributions first, or choose an extraction method that does not require normality.

Factors are statistical summaries of correlation, not discovered causes. A factor labelled 'economic confidence' is the analyst's reading of which variables load together, and a different rotation or sample may support a different label.

Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which have no single correct answer and can change both which variables group together and how readable the factors are. Report the choices made and check that the structure is stable.
Requires a sample that is large relative to the number of variables. With small samples the loadings are unstable and change when a few cases are added or removed.

Describes the structure of the data fed into it, not how a trained model uses that data. Factors of a model's inputs say nothing about which factors the model relies on, unless the model is also built on or analysed with the factor scores.

resources.title: Overview and confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis of AI literacy scale
resources.abstract: Comprehensive concepts of AI literacy (AIL) and valid measures are essential for research (e.g., intervention studies) and practice (e.g., personnel selection/development) alike. To date, several scales have been published, sharing standard features but differing in some aspects. We first aim to briefly overview instruments identified from unsystematic literature research in February 2023. We identified four scales and one collection of items. We describe the instruments and compare them. We identified common themes and overlaps in the instruments and developmental procedure. We also found differences regarding scale development procedures and latent dimensions. Following this literature research, we came to the conclusion that the literature on AI literacy measurement was fragmented, and little effort was undertaken to integrate different AI literacy conceptualizations. The second focus of this study is to test the factorial structures of existing AIL measurement instruments and identify latent dimensions of AIL across all instruments. We used robust maximum-likelihood confirmatory factor analysis to test factorial structures in a joint survey of all AIL items in an English-speaking online sample ( N =219). We found general support for all instruments' factorial structures with minor deviations from the original factorial structures for some of the instruments. In a second analysis step, to address the issue of fragmented research on AI literacy conceptualization and measurement, we used principal axis exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation to identify latent dimensions across all items. We found four correlated latent dimensions of AIL, which were mostly interpretable as the abilities to use and interact with AI, to design/program AI (incl. in-depth technical knowledge), to perform complex cognitive operations regarding AI (e.g., ethical considerations), and a common factor for the abilities to detect AI/differentiate between AI and humans and manage persuasive influences of AI (i.e., persuasion literacy). Our findings sort the multitude of AIL instruments and reveal four latent core dimensions of AIL. Thus, they contribute importantly to the conceptual understanding of AIL that has been fragmented so far. • We give an overview of AI literacy measures. • Their factorial structures were mostly confirmed. • PA EFA identified four correlated latent dimensions across all instruments.

techniques.name: Principal Component Analysis
techniques.description: Principal component analysis (PCA) summarises a dataset that has many numeric features by finding a few new axes along which the data varies most. Each axis, called a principal component, is a weighted mix of the original features. The first axis follows the direction of greatest spread in the data, the second follows the greatest remaining spread at right angles to the first, and so on. Plotting the data on the first two or three axes gives a view of its structure, and the weights show which features move together.

example_use_cases.description: A retail analyst runs PCA on three dozen customer behaviour measures and finds that two components account for most of the variation. The weights show that one axis mixes spend and basket size and the other mixes visit frequency and recency, which gives the team a short list of dimensions to examine before building a segmentation model.

A team building a face verification system runs PCA on its training images and displays the leading components as images. If those components mainly capture lighting or background rather than face shape, the team knows the dataset's main variation reflects how the photos were taken, and can change what it collects.

A researcher auditing a word embedding takes the difference vectors for ten gendered word pairs, such as he and she, and runs PCA. The first component explains far more variance than the rest and far more than for random vectors, which suggests the embedding encodes gender mostly along one direction (Bolukbasi et al., 2016).

limitations.description: Each component mixes many original features, so it often has no clear real-world meaning, and the weights are hard to read when there are many features.
PCA captures only linear structure, so it can miss curved or clustered patterns in the data and interactions between features.

Results depend on feature scaling. PCA centres the data but does not rescale it, so a feature measured in large units can dominate the leading components. Standardise features first, or the components may reflect units and not structure.

PCA ranks directions by how much the data varies, not by how much they matter for an outcome. A high-variance component may be noise or irrelevant to a decision, and a low-variance one may carry the signal that separates classes, so leading components are not a guide to what a model needs.

Dropping components discards the variance they carry. Deciding how many to keep is a judgement call, for example a target share of variance explained, and it trades a simpler summary against lost detail.

resources.title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

techniques.name: t-SNE
techniques.description: t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding) turns high-dimensional data into a two- or three-dimensional map that can be plotted and inspected. It is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method, so it can unfold curved structure that linear methods such as principal component analysis, which find only straight-line directions of greatest variation, would flatten. For each pair of points it works out how likely they are to be neighbours in the original space. It then moves the points around on the map until the same neighbour probabilities hold there as closely as possible. Because it concentrates on keeping near neighbours together, clusters of similar items usually appear as visible groups, whether the points are raw data or a model's internal representations such as embeddings.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group maps the gene-expression profiles of several thousand tumour samples with t-SNE and checks whether samples of the same clinical subtype form groups before training a subtype classifier. Subtypes that overlap on the map tell the team where the classifier is likely to confuse them.

An image-classification team maps the final hidden-layer activations of a trained network with t-SNE, colouring points by predicted class. It checks whether cars, animals and furniture fall into separate regions and which classes the network places close together, before reviewing misclassifications.

A trust-and-safety team maps the sentence embeddings used by a content-moderation model, colouring each post by the moderators' label. It checks whether flagged posts form their own group or sit among harmless posts on the same topic, and so decides whether the embedding needs retraining.

limitations.description: Results depend on random initialisation and a non-convex optimisation, so separate runs can lay clusters out differently. Fix the random seed, or start from a principal component analysis, and compare several runs before drawing conclusions.
Only local neighbourhoods are reliably preserved. Cluster sizes and the gaps between clusters carry no dependable meaning, so reading distance between groups as similarity will mislead a reviewer.

Perplexity (roughly the number of neighbours each point considers) and the number of iterations change the picture a great deal. Low settings can make random noise look like clusters, so a single plot at a single setting is weak evidence.
Standard t-SNE needs time and memory that grow with the square of the number of points, so datasets beyond roughly 10,000 points need an approximate variant or a subsample.

resources.title: Visualizing Data using t-SNE
resources.abstract:
We present a new technique called "t-SNE" that visualizes
high-dimensional data by giving each datapoint a location in a two or
three-dimensional map. The technique is a variation of Stochastic
Neighbor Embedding (Hinton and Roweis, 2002) that is much easier to optimize,
and produces significantly better visualizations by reducing the
tendency to crowd points together in the center of the map. t-SNE is
better than existing techniques at creating a single map that reveals
structure at many different scales. This is particularly important for
high-dimensional data that lie on several different, but related,
low-dimensional manifolds, such as images ofobjects from multiple
classes seen from multiple viewpoints. For visualizing the structure
of very large data sets, we show how t-SNE can use random walks on
neighborhood graphs to allow the implicit structure of all of the data
to influence the way in which a subset of the data is displayed. We
illustrate the performance of t-SNE on a wide variety of data sets and
compare it with many other non-parametric visualization techniques,
including Sammon mapping, Isomap, and Locally Linear Embedding. The
visualizations produced by t-SNE are significantly better than those
produced by the other techniques on almost all of the data sets.

resources.title: The art of using t-SNE for single-cell transcriptomics
resources.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics yields ever growing data sets containing RNA expression levels for thousands of genes from up to millions of cells. Common data analysis pipelines include a dimensionality reduction step for visualising the data in two dimensions, most frequently performed using t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). It excels at revealing local structure in high-dimensional data, but naive applications often suffer from severe shortcomings, e.g. the global structure of the data is not represented accurately. Here we describe how to circumvent such pitfalls, and develop a protocol for creating more faithful t-SNE visualisations. It includes PCA initialisation, a high learning rate, and multi-scale similarity kernels; for very large data sets, we additionally use exaggeration and downsampling-based initialisation. We use published single-cell RNA-seq data sets to demonstrate that this protocol yields superior results compared to the naive application of t-SNE.

resources.title: Automated optimized parameters for T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding improve visualization and analysis of large datasets
resources.abstract: Accurate and comprehensive extraction of information from high-dimensional single cell datasets necessitates faithful visualizations to assess biological populations. A state-of-the-art algorithm for non-linear dimension reduction, t-SNE, requires multiple heuristics and fails to produce clear representations of datasets when millions of cells are projected. We develop opt-SNE, an automated toolkit for t-SNE parameter selection that utilizes Kullback-Leibler divergence evaluation in real time to tailor the early exaggeration and overall number of gradient descent iterations in a dataset-specific manner. The precise calibration of early exaggeration together with opt-SNE adjustment of gradient descent learning rate dramatically improves computation time and enables high-quality visualization of large cytometry and transcriptomics datasets, overcoming limitations of analysis tools with hard-coded parameters that often produce poorly resolved or misleading maps of fluorescent and mass cytometry data. In summary, opt-SNE enables superior data resolution in t-SNE space and thereby more accurate data interpretation.

techniques.name: Prototype and Criticism Models
techniques.description: Prototype and criticism methods summarise a dataset with a small set of real examples. Prototypes are instances chosen to represent the bulk of the data, so that together they match its overall distribution as closely as possible. Criticisms are the instances the prototypes represent worst, which shows what the summary leaves out. In a set of customer transactions, prototypes might be the usual buying patterns and criticisms might be bulk buyers or one-off high-value customers. A reviewer can read a few dozen examples instead of the whole dataset, but the method describes the data only, so how a model performs on the unusual cases needs a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology team summarises a medical imaging dataset with prototypes and criticisms. The prototypes show the typical scans that dominate the data, and the criticisms show rare presentations the data covers thinly. The team uses the criticisms to choose cases for a separate check of how accurate the model is on rare presentations.

A credit risk team summarises its borrower records with prototypes (typical low-risk profiles) and criticisms (unusual but legitimate patterns, such as irregular self-employed income). It passes the criticism cases to a separate accuracy check, to see whether the scoring model handles them as well as typical borrowers.

An engineer preparing a visual inspection model for a production line computes prototypes and criticisms for each defect class on the model's image embeddings. The criticisms show unusual captures, such as odd lighting or partial views, which the team adds to the test set so the model is checked on them.

limitations.description: Which examples are chosen depends on the similarity measure and its settings, so different reasonable choices give different prototypes and criticisms. The original paper lists the effect of the kernel choice as future work, so there is no settled guidance.
The method needs a similarity score between every pair of examples, so memory and time grow with the square of the dataset size. Large datasets may need to be sampled before the method is run.
The user sets the number of prototypes and criticisms. Too few leaves large parts of the data unrepresented, and too many defeats the purpose of a summary short enough for a person to read.

It describes the data, not the model. Criticisms are the examples the prototypes represent worst, which is not the same as the examples the model gets wrong, so a separate evaluation is needed to learn how the model performs on them.

The original evidence that criticisms help people understand a dataset is a pilot study with four participants. Those who saw prototypes and criticisms were more accurate but slower than those who saw prototypes alone, so the benefit for a given audience is untested.

resources.title: Examples are not Enough, Learn to Criticize! Criticism for Interpretability
resources.abstract: Example-based explanations are widely used in the effort to improve the interpretability of highly complex distributions. However, prototypes alone are rarely sufficient to represent the gist of the complexity. In order for users to construct better mental models and understand complex data distributions, we also need criticism to explain what are not captured by prototypes. Motivated by the Bayesian model criticism framework, we develop MMD-critic which efficiently learns prototypes and criticism, designed to aid human interpretability. A human subject pilot study shows that the MMD-critic selects prototypes and criticism that are useful to facilitate human understanding and reasoning. We also evaluate the prototypes selected by MMD-critic via a nearest prototype classifier, showing competitive performance compared to baselines.

resources.title: Prototype selection for interpretable classification
resources.abstract: Prototype methods seek a minimal subset of samples that can serve as a distillation or condensed view of a data set. As the size of modern data sets grows, being able to present a domain specialist with a short list of "representative" samples chosen from the data set is of increasing interpretative value. While much recent statistical research has been focused on producing sparse-in-the-variables methods, this paper aims at achieving sparsity in the samples. We discuss a method for selecting prototypes in the classification setting (in which the samples fall into known discrete categories). Our method of focus is derived from three basic properties that we believe a good prototype set should satisfy. This intuition is translated into a set cover optimization problem, which we solve approximately using standard approaches. While prototype selection is usually viewed as purely a means toward building an efficient classifier, in this paper we emphasize the inherent value of having a set of prototypical elements. That said, by using the nearest-neighbor rule on the set of prototypes, we can of course discuss our method as a classifier as well.

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

techniques.name: ANCHOR
techniques.description: ANCHOR explains one prediction of a black-box classifier with an if-then rule, called an anchor, such as 'age > 30 AND income < £50k'. An anchor names a small set of feature conditions under which the model keeps giving the same prediction, whatever the other features are. To find one, the method fixes the conditions, varies the other features by sampling, asks the model for a prediction each time, and searches for the broadest rule that holds in at least a chosen share of the samples, commonly 95%. Each anchor comes with its estimated precision and its coverage, the share of cases to which it applies. Both figures describe the model's behaviour on the sampled variations, not on real cases, and continuous features are first grouped into ranges.

example_use_cases.description: A model-validation team at a lender computes anchors for a sample of declined applications from a gradient-boosted credit model. It checks that the conditions holding each decision, such as a low credit-score band together with recent missed payments, match credit policy, and reads each rule's coverage to see how many other applications it applies to.

A hospital data team explains individual alerts from a tabular sepsis-risk model with anchors, and a clinician checks whether the conditions in each rule, such as raised temperature and white-cell count, are clinically sensible or point to an artefact such as the ward an admission came from.

An employer's compliance team gives a reviewer the anchor behind a shortlisting prediction, with its precision and coverage. The reviewer tests the rule on other applications and can challenge it if it leans on an attribute that should not matter, such as age.

limitations.description: The stated precision is measured on perturbed samples from a chosen sampling distribution, not on real cases. If that distribution produces unrealistic inputs, or is skewed by an unbalanced training set, the figure can overstate how far the rule can be relied on.

An anchor covers only the inputs its conditions match, often a small share. In the original experiments average coverage ranged from about 1% to 29% on tabular data, so one anchor says little about the model as a whole. Choosing a set of anchors helps but adds effort.

Predictions close to the model's decision boundary, or of rare classes, need long, very specific rules with little coverage, which add little insight. Strict precision thresholds make this more likely.

Continuous features must be grouped into ranges before rules can be stated, and the grouping changes which anchors are found. Too coarse hides boundaries, and too fine gives narrow rules with little coverage.

Each anchor needs many queries to the model, so run time depends on how fast the model is and on the number of features. The method is built for classifiers, so a numeric output must first be turned into classes.

resources.title: Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
resources.abstract: We introduce a novel model-agnostic system that explains the behavior of complex models with high-precision rules called anchors, representing local, "sufficient" conditions for predictions. We propose an algorithm to efficiently compute these explanations for any black-box model with high-probability guarantees. We demonstrate the flexibility of anchors by explaining a myriad of different models for different domains and tasks. In a user study, we show that anchors enable users to predict how a model would behave on unseen instances with less effort and higher precision, as compared to existing linear explanations or no explanations.

resources.title: Interpretability in HealthCare A Comparative Study of Local Machine Learning Interpretability Techniques
resources.abstract: Although complex machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Neural Networks) are commonly outperforming the traditional simple interpretable models (e.g., Linear Regression, Decision Tree), in the healthcare domain, clinicians find it hard to understand and trust these complex models due to the lack of intuition and explanation of their predictions. With the new General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the importance for plausibility and verifiability of the predictions made by machine learning models has become essential. To tackle this challenge, recently, several machine learning interpretability techniques have been developed and introduced. In general, the main aim of these interpretability techniques is to shed light and provide insights into the predictions process of the machine learning models and explain how the model predictions have resulted. However, in practice, assessing the quality of the explanations provided by the various interpretability techniques is still questionable. In this paper, we present a comprehensive experimental evaluation of three recent and popular local model agnostic interpretability techniques, namely, LIME, SHAP and Anchors on different types of real-world healthcare data. Our experimental evaluation covers different aspects for its comparison including identity, stability, separability, similarity, execution time and bias detection. The results of our experiments show that LIME achieves the lowest performance for the identity metric and the highest performance for the separability metric across all datasets included in this study. On average, SHAP has the smallest average time to output explanation across all datasets included in this study. For detecting the bias, SHAP enables the participants to better detect the bias.

sample_claims.text: For a sample of declined loan applications, each decision of the credit model is held in place by a short rule over policy-relevant features, with estimated precision of at least 95% under the stated sampling distribution.

Sepsis alerts raised by the risk model are each explained by a rule over clinical measurements, and a clinician reviewed a sample of rules and found none that relies on an administrative field such as ward or admission time.
The set of rules chosen to explain the classifier covers at least half of the validation cases, so the main patterns it relies on have been examined.
Each shortlisting decision from the screening model can be given to a reviewer as a rule with its precision and coverage, so that the reviewer can test the rule on other applications.
Every reason given for an individual model output states its own coverage, so a reviewer knows which other cases the reason applies to and which it does not.

techniques.name: RuleFit
techniques.description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A telecoms analytics team fits RuleFit to the predictions of its gradient-boosted churn model rather than to the churn labels, to get a short list of rules that approximates the model. Marketing staff read the top rules, and the team reports how closely the rules reproduce the model's predictions before anyone relies on them.

A lender replaces an opaque default-risk model with a RuleFit model fitted to repayment outcomes. For one declined application, the importance scores show which few rules and income or debt terms drove its score, and the validation team checks them against credit policy.

A hospital team builds an admission-risk model as a RuleFit model fitted directly to patient outcomes, so that clinicians and the ethics committee can read the whole model, a few rules such as 'IF systolic_bp > 140 AND diabetes = true' plus a handful of weights. The team counts the active rules first and keeps the model only if it is short enough to read.

limitations.description: The lasso can leave many rules active, and a model with hundreds of active terms is no longer readable. Rules also approximate smooth linear trends poorly and need many pieces to do so. Count the non-zero terms before calling the model interpretable.

Rules overlap and are often correlated, so a rule's weight cannot be read on its own. 'Temperature above 15' is also true wherever 'temperature above 10' is. With correlated inputs, rules can also suggest interactions that are not in the real relationship.

Tree size sets how long rules can be and which interactions can appear. Shallow trees give short, readable rules but miss high-order interactions, and deep trees capture them at the cost of long rules. No single depth suits every problem.

Fitted to a black-box model's predictions, RuleFit only approximates that model. Without a fidelity check, such as agreement on held-out inputs, its rules describe the surrogate and may not describe the model they are meant to explain.

resources.title: Predictive learning via rule ensembles
resources.abstract: General regression and classification models are constructed as linear combinations of simple rules derived from the data. Each rule consists of a conjunction of a small number of simple statements concerning the values of individual input variables. These rule ensembles are shown to produce predictive accuracy comparable to the best methods. However, their principal advantage lies in interpretation. Because of its simple form, each rule is easy to understand, as is its influence on individual predictions, selected subsets of predictions, or globally over the entire space of joint input variable values. Similarly, the degree of relevance of the respective input variables can be assessed globally, locally in different regions of the input space, or at individual prediction points. Techniques are presented for automatically identifying those variables that are involved in interactions with other variables, the strength and degree of those interactions, as well as the identities of the other variables with which they interact. Graphical representations are used to visualize both main and interaction effects.

resources.title: RuleFit-Based Nomogram Using Inflammatory Indicators for Predicting Survival in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, a Bi-Center Study
resources.abstract: Purpose: Traditional prognostic studies utilized different cut-off values, without evaluating potential information contained in inflammation-related hematological indicators. Using the interpretable machine-learning algorithm RuleFit, this study aimed to explore valuable inflammatory rules reflecting prognosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patients. Patients and Methods: In total, 1706 biopsy-proven NPC patients treated in two independent hospitals (1320 and 386) between January 2010 and March 2014 were included. RuleFit was used to develop risk-predictive rules using hematological indicators with no distributive difference between the two centers. Time-event-dependent hematological rules were further selected by stepwise multivariate Cox analysis. Combining high-efficiency hematological rules and clinical predictors, a final model was established. Models based on other algorithms (AutoML, Lasso) and clinical predictors were built for comparison, as well as a reported nomogram. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and concordance index (C-index) were used to verify the predictive precision of different models. A site-based app was established for convenience. Results: RuleFit identified 22 combined baseline hematological rules, achieving AUROCs of 0.69 and 0.64 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. By contrast, the AUROCs of the optimal contrast model based on AutoML were 1.00 and 0.58. For overall survival, the final model had a much higher C-index than the base model using TN staging in two cohorts (0.769 vs 0.717, P < 0.001; 0.752 vs 0.688, P < 0.001), and showing great generalizability in training and validation cohorts. The two models based on RuleFit rules performed best, compared with other models. As for other endpoints, the final model showed a similar trend. Kaplan–Meier curve exhibited 22.9% (390/1706) patients were “misclassified” by AJCC staging, but the final model could assess risk classification accurately. Conclusion: The proposed final models based on inflammation-related rules based on RuleFit showed significantly elevated predictive performance.

sample_claims.text: The credit risk model's decision logic is expressible as a sparse set of interpretable if-then rules combined with linear feature weights
The patient risk score can be reconstructed from its intercept, active clinical-input rules and linear terms using the recorded clipping and weights.

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Neuron Activation Analysis
techniques.description: Neuron activation analysis examines when individual neurons in a neural network respond strongly. The analyst runs a set of inputs through the model, finds the inputs that activate a chosen neuron most and least, and looks for the concept that separates them, such as buildings in an image classifier or French text in a language model. Some methods test the match automatically, for example by scoring how closely a neuron's activation lines up with labelled examples of a concept. The result is a list of neurons with candidate meanings and the evidence behind each. These meanings are correlations between inputs and activations, so they show what a neuron responds to, not what it does to the model's output.

example_use_cases.description: An ML team inspects a scene classifier trained to sort building and street images. For each neuron in a late layer they compare the images that activate it most with those that do not, using object labels from the dataset. Some neurons line up with a clear concept such as a building and others only weakly, which tells the team how much of the layer can be read.

A hospital assurance team examines a clinical language model and finds neurons whose strongest activations come from text about a particular drug class or condition. A clinician reviews whether the concepts are the expected ones. The finding shows which clinical concepts the model represents internally, not that these neurons cause any particular suggestion.

limitations.description: Many neurons respond to several unrelated concepts, or play different roles depending on the surrounding input. A single label such as 'toxic language' can then be wrong or only part of the story, and consistent interpretation across scenarios is hard.

Behaviour is often spread across many neurons instead of held in one, so a neuron-by-neuron view can miss it. Checking combinations of neurons is much harder than checking single ones, and the number of combinations grows quickly.

The analysis shows which inputs make a neuron fire, not what the neuron contributes to the output. Showing that a neuron matters needs a separate experiment that switches it off or alters it and measures the effect.

A neuron can only be matched to concepts the analyst has examples for. In image models this means a densely labelled dataset, and a neuron whose concept is missing from it goes unexplained or is mislabelled.

The method needs access to the model's internal activations, so it cannot be used on a model reached only through an API. Large language models have hundreds of thousands of neurons or more, so in practice only a chosen subset can be examined and labelled with care.
